studies.Reference: Soy food and isoflavone intake and endometrial cancer risk: the Japan Public Health Center-based prospective study.
studies.Authors: Budhathoki S, Iwasaki M, Sawada N, Yamaji T, Shimazu T, Sasazuki S, Inoue M, Tsugane S,
studies.Journal: BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Intakes of soy foods as well as other covariates were assessed in 1995-1998 by a self-administered food frequency questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Forty nine thousand one hundred and twenty-one women of age 45-74 years who responded to a 5-year follow-up survey questionnaire.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: The multivariate-adjusted HR per 25 g/day increase in the intake of soy food was 1.02 (95% CI 0.94-1.10)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: we observed no evidence of a protective association between soy food or isoflavone intake and endometrial cancer risk.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Incidence of endometrial cancer. During an average of 12.1 years of follow up, 112 newly diagnosed endometrial cancer cases were identified.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Intakes of soy foods as well as other covariates were assessed in 1995-1998 by a self-administered food frequency questionnaire.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Insufficient studies to perform formal publication bias testing.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 0.75 (95% CI: 0.37–1.51), indicating no statistically significant association between soy and uterine cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 85.13%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
